Tutorial 4: CRISPR-Cas9 screens

Emanuel Michele Soda

Istituto Europeo Oncologia (IEO), Milano, Italy
emanuelsoda@gmail.com

Elena Ceccacci

Istituto Europeo Oncologia (IEO), Milano, Italy
elena.ceccacci@ieo.it

2026-10-17

Source: vignettes/Tutorial_4_CRISPR_screens.Rmd
Tutorial_4_CRISPR_screens.Rmd

About this tutorial

ScreenR was written for shRNA screens, but CRISPR-Cas9 knockout screens produce the same kind of data: a table of read counts, one row for each guide RNA (sgRNA) and one column for each sample. In ScreenR an sgRNA is simply a “barcode”, and everything in the other tutorials applies. This tutorial goes through a CRISPR dropout screen step by step and shows what is specific to CRISPR:

  1. installing ScreenR and, optionally, CRISPRcleanR;
  2. describing a time-course dropout screen (T0 and later time points);
  3. choosing the thresholds on the number of sgRNAs per gene;
  4. checking the quality of the screen with essential and non-essential reference genes;
  5. correcting the copy-number bias of CRISPR-Cas9 with CRISPRcleanR;
  6. finding the hits, using the non-essential genes as reference;
  7. positive-selection screens.
shRNA screen CRISPR-Cas9 knockout screen
Reagent (a “barcode” in ScreenR) shRNA sgRNA
Reagents per gene often 5 to 25 usually 3 to 6 (4 in TKOv3 and Brunello)
Typical design treated vs control at each time point late time point vs T0 or plasmid
Gene-independent effects seed (off-target) effects DNA cutting: copy-number and proximity bias
Good null reference non-essential genes non-essential genes (non-targeting sgRNAs do not cut, so they are not a good null)

Installation

ScreenR is on Bioconductor:

if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages("BiocManager")
}
BiocManager::install("ScreenR")

The copy-number correction uses the CRISPRcleanR package (Iorio et al. 2018). It is optional: everything else in this tutorial works without it. CRISPRcleanR is not on CRAN or Bioconductor, so it is installed from GitHub; BiocManager::install() also installs its Bioconductor dependencies:

BiocManager::install("francescojm/CRISPRcleanR")

crisprcleanr_available() tells whether it is installed:

library(ScreenR)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
crisprcleanr_available()

CRISPRcleanR is not installed where this tutorial was built: the code of the copy-number correction is shown but not run, and its results are read from a precomputed table.

The data

hap1_count_table comes from a genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 knockout screen of HAP1 cells with the TKOv3 library (Hart et al. 2017): the T0 sample and three replicates after 3 and 18 days of growth. Cells that lose a gene needed for growth (an essential gene) are lost over time, so the sgRNAs of essential genes are depleted at day 18. To keep the package small the dataset is a subset of the 70,877 sgRNAs of the library (see ?hap1_count_table).

data(hap1_count_table)
data(hap1_annotation_table)
head(hap1_count_table)
#>                     Barcode  T0 T3_A T3_B T3_C T18_A T18_B T18_C
#> 1 EGFP_TGGTTGTCGGGCAGCAGCAC 537  222  150  216   243   115   304
#> 2 EGFP_GGTTGTCGGGCAGCAGCACG 210  197   92  125   195   177   115
#> 3 EGFP_TTCAAGTCCGCCATGCCCGA 517  423  255  282   329   309   433
#> 4 EGFP_CGGCGGTCACGAACTCCAGC 278  167   54  120   165   184    65
#> 5 EGFP_GGTGCCCATCCTGGTCGAGC  83   99   41   19   107   103    44
#> 6 EGFP_GAAGTTCGAGGGCGACACCC 268  145  153  204   133   295   228
head(hap1_annotation_table)
#>                     Barcode Gene Chromosome Strand Start End   Class
#> 1 EGFP_TGGTTGTCGGGCAGCAGCAC EGFP       <NA>   <NA>    NA  NA control
#> 2 EGFP_GGTTGTCGGGCAGCAGCACG EGFP       <NA>   <NA>    NA  NA control
#> 3 EGFP_TTCAAGTCCGCCATGCCCGA EGFP       <NA>   <NA>    NA  NA control
#> 4 EGFP_CGGCGGTCACGAACTCCAGC EGFP       <NA>   <NA>    NA  NA control
#> 5 EGFP_GGTGCCCATCCTGGTCGAGC EGFP       <NA>   <NA>    NA  NA control
#> 6 EGFP_GAAGTTCGAGGGCGACACCC EGFP       <NA>   <NA>    NA  NA control

The annotation has the gene of each sgRNA and its position in the genome (used by CRISPRcleanR), and a Class column that tells the core essential and non-essential reference genes, the controls and the other genes.

Creating the ScreenR object

The sample names (T0, T3_A, …) do not follow the Day_Treatment_Replicate convention of ScreenR, so the samples are described with a sample_table. In a dropout screen the comparison is between time points, so all the samples belong to the same experiment (Day = "Screen") and the time point is used as the Treatment; the groups (used by the statistical models) are the time points too.

samples <- data.frame(
    Sample = colnames(hap1_count_table)[-1],
    Day = "Screen",
    Treatment = c("T0", "T3", "T3", "T3", "T18", "T18", "T18")
)
samples
#>   Sample    Day Treatment
#> 1     T0 Screen        T0
#> 2   T3_A Screen        T3
#> 3   T3_B Screen        T3
#> 4   T3_C Screen        T3
#> 5  T18_A Screen       T18
#> 6  T18_B Screen       T18
#> 7  T18_C Screen       T18
object <- create_screenr_object(
    table = hap1_count_table,
    annotation = hap1_annotation_table,
    groups = factor(samples$Treatment, levels = c("T0", "T3", "T18")),
    sample_table = samples
)
object <- remove_all_zero_row(object)
object
#> class: screenr_object 
#> dim: 13598 7 
#> metadata(1): screenr_layout
#> assays(1): counts
#> rownames(13598): EGFP_TGGTTGTCGGGCAGCAGCAC EGFP_GGTTGTCGGGCAGCAGCACG
#>   ... luciferase_GGCTATGAAGAGATACGCCC luciferase_GGCATGCGAGAATCTGACGC
#> rowData names(7): Barcode Gene ... End Class
#> colnames(7): T0 T3_A ... T18_B T18_C
#> colData names(4): Sample Day Treatment Group
#> normalization: none (run normalize_data())

How many sgRNAs per gene?

Several functions test a gene only if it has enough barcodes: number_barcode in find_camera_hit(), find_roast_hit(), find_time_hit() and plot_barcode_hit() (genes need more than number_barcode barcodes, default 3) and min_barcodes in find_gene_zscore_hit() (genes need at least min_barcodes, default 3). These defaults were chosen for shRNA libraries. barcodes_per_gene() shows what the library has:

per_gene <- barcodes_per_gene(object)
table(per_gene$NBarcodes)
#> 
#>    1    2    3    4   22   24   94 
#>   52   51   88 3260    1    1    1

Most genes have 4 sgRNAs. With number_barcode = 3, genes that lost one sgRNA (and genes designed with 3) are not tested; when this excludes many genes the functions give a warning that suggests a better value, so it is safe to start from the defaults. Here number_barcode = 2 (at least 3 sgRNAs) keeps almost every gene.

Quality control

The general quality control of Tutorial 2 applies to CRISPR screens, with any sample names and time points.

Sequencing depth

plot_mapped_reads() shows the number of reads of each sample. Samples with far fewer reads than the others are less reliable:

plot_mapped_reads(object)

The T0 sample was sequenced about twice as deeply as the others, which is common: it is the reference of every comparison. Every sample has at least 1.6 million reads, more than 100 for each sgRNA of this subset.

plot_mapped_reads_distribution() shows the distribution of the reads of the sgRNAs in each sample:

plot_mapped_reads_distribution(object)

plot_mapped_reads_distribution(object, type = "density", alpha = 0.3)

The counts are raw, so the T0 sample, sequenced more deeply, is shifted to the right. At day 18 the distribution is wider than at day 3, with more sgRNAs close to 0: the sgRNAs of the essential genes are dropping out.

Library representation and replicates

The library should be evenly represented at T0 (low Gini index) and the replicates should agree:

plot_gini(object)

The plots so far use the raw counts. The correlation between replicates and the sample plots below compare normalized counts, so the counts are normalized first (counts per million; the choice of the normalization is discussed below):

object <- normalize_data(object)
plot_replicate_correlation(object)

Clustering of the samples

plot_mds() and plot_pca() place the samples so that similar samples are close, and plot_explained_variance() shows how much of the differences between the samples each principal component explains. Both the MDS and the PCA use the log2 normalized counts, with the normalization chosen in normalize_data() (here counts per million), so that the sequencing depth of the samples does not drive the result:

plot_mds(object)

plot_pca(object)

plot_explained_variance(object)

plot_explained_variance(object, cumulative = TRUE)

The first dimension of both plots orders the samples by time point (T0, then day 3, then day 18): the main difference between the samples is the growth of the cells, as expected in a dropout screen. The day 3 replicates are very close; the day 18 replicates differ more, because the depletion has had more time to diverge. The first principal component explains 59% of the variability.

Quality with reference genes

The most informative check of a dropout screen uses genes whose behaviour is known: the core essential genes should be depleted, the non-essential genes should not. hart_reference_genes has the lists of Hart et al. for human cells. compute_screen_quality() measures how well the two groups are separated (NNMD and Cohen’s d: more negative is better; ROC AUC: 0.5 is no separation, 1 is perfect) and plot_reference_separation() shows it.

data(hart_reference_genes)
essential <- hart_reference_genes$Gene[
    hart_reference_genes$Class == "core essential"]
nonessential <- hart_reference_genes$Gene[
    hart_reference_genes$Class == "non-essential"]

compute_metrics() computes the log2 fold change of each sgRNA between two groups of samples (control and treatment are values of the Treatment column):

day3 <- compute_metrics(object,
    control = "T0", treatment = "T3", day = "Screen"
)
day18 <- compute_metrics(object,
    control = "T0", treatment = "T18", day = "Screen"
)
quality <- bind_rows(
    `Day 3` = compute_screen_quality(day3, essential, nonessential),
    `Day 18` = compute_screen_quality(day18, essential, nonessential),
    .id = "Time point"
)
knitr::kable(quality, digits = 3)
Time point NEssential NNonessential MeanEssential MeanNonessential NNMD CohenD AUC
Day 3 646 797 -0.722 0.178 -2.510 -1.604 0.881
Day 18 646 797 -2.346 0.358 -7.199 -3.868 0.998

After 3 days the essential genes are only starting to drop out; after 18 days the separation is almost perfect.

plot_reference_separation(day18, essential, nonessential) +
    ggtitle("Day 18 vs T0")

plot_boxplot() shows the normalized counts of the sgRNAs of single genes in each sample, for example two core essential genes and the EGFP control (sgRNAs that target a gene not present in the cells):

plot_boxplot(object,
    genes = c("POLR2L", "RPL14", "EGFP"),
    group_var = c("T0", "T3", "T18"), fill_var = "Treatment", ncol = 3
) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

The sgRNAs of the essential genes are depleted at day 3 and almost gone at day 18; those of EGFP are stable (slightly higher, because of the CPM normalization described below).

The non-essential genes have a positive mean log2 fold change (0.36 at day 18) although they have no effect. This is a side effect of the CPM normalization: when many sgRNAs drop out, the reads of the sample go to the others, which look enriched. The ranking of the genes does not change, but the baseline is not 0. Normalizing to the sgRNAs of the non-essential genes (method = "control") puts it back at 0:

nonessential_sgrnas <- hap1_annotation_table$Barcode[
    hap1_annotation_table$Gene %in% nonessential]
day18_control <- normalize_data(object,
    method = "control", control_barcodes = nonessential_sgrnas
) %>%
    compute_metrics(control = "T0", treatment = "T18", day = "Screen")
#> Warning: 1 of the 3067 control barcodes are not in the object
#> (OTOP3_TCTCCGGAAAGCTTCACACG): the other 3066 are used.
knitr::kable(compute_screen_quality(day18_control, essential, nonessential),
    digits = 3)
NEssential NNonessential MeanEssential MeanNonessential NNMD CohenD AUC
646 797 -2.782 0.027 -7.184 -3.688 0.997

Copy-number bias and CRISPRcleanR

Cas9 cuts the DNA, and cells with many cuts grow less. sgRNAs that target amplified regions of the genome therefore deplete the cells whatever the gene they target, and the genes there look essential. CRISPRcleanR (Iorio et al. 2018) finds the regions where many neighbouring sgRNAs that target different genes are depleted together and corrects their fold changes, without needing copy-number data. correct_crispr_bias() runs CRISPRcleanR on a ScreenR object and returns a new ScreenR object with the corrected counts. ScreenR does not reimplement the method: it only calls CRISPRcleanR.

The correction needs

  • the complete genome-wide library: CRISPRcleanR assumes that most of the genes in a region have no effect. On a subset of genes enriched in hits it removes real signal, so it must not be used on hap1_count_table;
  • a library annotation with the position of each sgRNA, in the format of CRISPRcleanR (row names: the sgRNA identifiers; columns GENES, CHRM, STARTpos and ENDpos). CRISPRcleanR includes the annotation of several libraries (KY_Library_v1.0, Brunello_Library, AVANA_Library, GeCKO_Library_v2, …); for another library, build the data frame from its annotation file.

This example uses the complete HT-29 screen distributed with CRISPRcleanR (KY library, about 90,000 sgRNAs; HT-29 cells carry an amplification of the MYC region on chromosome 8q24). It takes about a minute.

ccr <- "CRISPRcleanR"
# Library annotation and counts distributed with CRISPRcleanR
library_annotation <- get(utils::data("KY_Library_v1.0", package = ccr))
counts <- read.delim(system.file("extdata", "HT-29_counts.tsv",
    package = ccr
))
colnames(counts) <- c("Barcode", "Gene", "Plasmid", "HT29_R1", "HT29_R2",
    "HT29_R3")
ht29 <- create_screenr_object(
    table = counts[, -2], annotation = counts[, c("Barcode", "Gene")],
    groups = factor(c("Plasmid", "Late", "Late", "Late")),
    sample_table = data.frame(
        Sample = c("Plasmid", "HT29_R1", "HT29_R2", "HT29_R3"),
        Day = "Screen", Treatment = c("Plasmid", "Late", "Late", "Late")
    )
)
ht29_corrected <- correct_crispr_bias(ht29,
    library_annotation = library_annotation,
    control = "Plasmid", treatment = c("HT29_R1", "HT29_R2", "HT29_R3")
)
ht29_corrected

The corrected object is analysed like any other: normalize it, compute the data table and find the hits. CRISPRcleanR’s own results (the corrected sgRNA fold changes and the segments of the genome) are in S4Vectors::metadata(ht29_corrected)$crisprcleanr.

The effect of the correction on this screen (computed with the code above; the script is in the benchmark/crispr folder of the GitHub repository):

correction <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "crisprcleanr_ht29.csv",
    package = "ScreenR"
))
knitr::kable(correction, digits = 3,
    col.names = c("Counts", "NNMD", "Cohen's d", "ROC AUC",
        "Mean log2FC in 8q24 (genes not known to be essential)")
)
Counts NNMD Cohen’s d ROC AUC Mean log2FC in 8q24 (genes not known to be essential)
Raw -8.288 -2.947 0.994 -0.260
Corrected (CRISPRcleanR) -8.765 -2.617 0.979 0.019

Before the correction, the genes in the amplified 8q24 region that are not known to be essential are depleted (mean log2 fold change about -0.26); after the correction they are not (about 0). The separation of the reference genes is similar, with a slightly lower ROC AUC: the correction removes a gene-independent bias, it does not make the screen stronger.

Finding the hits

The hit-finding functions are used as in Tutorial 3. The comparison is day 18 against T0:

design <- create_design_matrix(object)
contrast <- create_contrast(design, treatment = "T18", control = "T0")

Gene-level Z-score test with the non-essential genes as reference

find_gene_zscore_hit() compares the mean score of the sgRNAs of each gene with the scores of random sets of sgRNAs. By default the random sgRNAs come from all the genes, which include the hits, so the test is conservative when many genes have an effect, as in proliferation screens. When genes known to have no effect are available, they are a better reference (control_genes). For CRISPR screens the non-essential genes are the natural choice: their sgRNAs cut the DNA like any other, while non-targeting sgRNAs do not.

To be able to check the result, here half of the non-essential genes are used as reference and the other half is kept to count the false calls; in a real analysis use all of them.

set.seed(2017)
reference <- sample(nonessential, length(nonessential) %/% 2)
held_out <- setdiff(nonessential, reference)
statistics <- compute_barcode_statistics(object, design, contrast)
zscore <- find_gene_zscore_hit(statistics,
    control_genes = reference, fdr = 1, seed = 1
)
head(zscore)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 6
#>   Gene   NBarcodes Score Log2FC     PValue       FDR
#>   <chr>      <int> <dbl>  <dbl>      <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 AARS           4 -2.73  -2.41 0.00001000 0.0000476
#> 2 ABCE1          4 -3.17  -3.15 0.00001000 0.0000476
#> 3 ABCF1          4 -2.37  -1.74 0.00001000 0.0000476
#> 4 ACTR10         4 -3.47  -3.18 0.00001000 0.0000476
#> 5 ACTR2          4 -2.94  -2.21 0.00001000 0.0000476
#> 6 ADSL           4 -3.52  -3.07 0.00001000 0.0000476
called <- zscore$Gene[zscore$FDR <= 0.05]
data.frame(
    `Genes called` = length(called),
    `Core essential` = sum(called %in% essential),
    `Held-out non-essential` = sum(called %in% held_out),
    `Other genes` = sum(!called %in% c(essential, nonessential)),
    check.names = FALSE
)
#>   Genes called Core essential Held-out non-essential Other genes
#> 1          911            619                      5         287

Almost all the 646 core essential genes of the dataset are found at 5% FDR, with very few of the held-out non-essential genes. The other genes called are not in the reference lists: HAP1 cells need many more genes than the core essential set, which contains only the genes essential in almost every cell line.

Without reference genes: the empirical null

When no reference genes are available, reference = "empirical" estimates the scores of the genes without effect from the data. Most genes have no effect, so the centre of the distribution of the gene statistics is the null; a normal distribution is fitted there and gives the p-values. The hits, in the tail, do not widen it. empirical_fit = "one-sided" estimates the spread from the side without hits only (above the centre for depleted genes), which gives more power when the hits are well separated, as in CRISPR screens; the default, "central", is the safer choice (see ?find_gene_zscore_hit).

zscore_empirical <- find_gene_zscore_hit(statistics,
    reference = "empirical", fdr = 1
)
zscore_one_sided <- find_gene_zscore_hit(statistics,
    reference = "empirical", empirical_fit = "one-sided", fdr = 1
)
attr(zscore_one_sided, "null")
#>      mean        sd 
#> 0.5670556 0.6900248

plot_empirical_null() shows the gene statistics and the fitted null, which should follow the centre of the distribution; the depleted genes are in the tail on the left:

plot_empirical_null(statistics, empirical_fit = "one-sided")

Other methods and their consensus

The other methods need no reference genes either: the default reference of the Z-score test (random sets of sgRNAs of all the genes), CAMERA and FRY. number_barcode = 2 keeps the genes with 3 or 4 sgRNAs.

zscore_default <- find_gene_zscore_hit(statistics, fdr = 1, seed = 1)
camera <- find_camera_hit(object, design, contrast,
    number_barcode = 2, fdr = 1
)
fry <- find_roast_hit(object, design, contrast,
    method = "fry", number_barcode = 2, fdr = 1
)
hit_list <- list(zscore_reference = zscore,
    zscore_empirical = zscore_empirical,
    zscore_one_sided = zscore_one_sided, zscore = zscore_default,
    camera = camera, fry = fry)
hits <- summarise_hits(hit_list, fdr = 0.05)
head(hits)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 10
#>   Gene    FDR_zscore_reference FDR_zscore_empirical FDR_zscore_one_sided
#>   <chr>                  <dbl>                <dbl>                <dbl>
#> 1 ATP6V1F            0.0000476         0.0000000236             4.47e-14
#> 2 BUB3               0.0000476         0.0000000130             1.47e-14
#> 3 CPSF1              0.0000476         0.0000000345             9.08e-14
#> 4 DHX15              0.0000476         0.0000000102             8.10e-15
#> 5 DPAGT1             0.0000476         0.0000000262             5.44e-14
#> 6 EIF3A              0.0000476         0.0000000101             6.35e-15
#> # ℹ 6 more variables: FDR_zscore <dbl>, FDR_camera <dbl>, FDR_fry <dbl>,
#> #   NMethods <dbl>, MaxFDR <dbl>, Hit <lgl>
table(hits$NMethods)
#> 
#>    0    1    2    3    4    5    6 
#> 2415   22   98  121  294   69  332
evaluate_hits <- function(result) {
    called <- result$Gene[result$FDR <= 0.05]
    data.frame(
        `Genes called` = length(called),
        `Core essential` = sum(called %in% essential),
        `Held-out non-essential` = sum(called %in% held_out),
        check.names = FALSE
    )
}
knitr::kable(bind_rows(lapply(hit_list, evaluate_hits), .id = "Method"))
Method Genes called Core essential Held-out non-essential
zscore_reference 911 619 5
zscore_empirical 798 596 3
zscore_one_sided 932 619 7
zscore 352 305 0
camera 381 326 0
fry 720 552 1

The empirical null finds almost as many core essential genes as the non-essential reference, without reference genes and with very few held-out non-essential genes. The two tests that compare each gene with all the others (the default Z-score test and CAMERA) are much more conservative: they find less than half of the core essential genes, and the default Z-score test does not give a p-value below 0.05 to any of the held-out non-essential genes. Their reference is all the genes of the library, and here it is full of hits: the subset keeps all the reference genes, so 19% of its genes are core essential, against about 4% in the complete TKOv3 library. They remain conservative on the complete library: there the default Z-score test found 58% of the core essential genes at 5% FDR, the empirical null 90% ("central") and 94% ("one-sided"), and the non-essential reference 96%. The default Z-score test and CAMERA rank the genes almost in the same way (Spearman correlation of the p-values above 0.99).

FRY (find_roast_hit()) tests each gene on its own sgRNAs. It estimates the variability from the replicates of the model, so a single T0 sample is enough when the other time points have replicates, as here. It finds more essential genes than the tests without reference, with very few held-out non-essential genes.

Comparable fold changes

scale_by_reference() scales the fold changes so that the non-essential genes are at 0 and the essential genes at -1. Scaled values can be compared between screens of different strength, for example between cell lines or time points:

scaled <- scale_by_reference(day18, essential, nonessential)
scaled %>%
    group_by(Gene) %>%
    summarise(ScaledLog2FC = mean(ScaledLog2FC)) %>%
    arrange(ScaledLog2FC) %>%
    head()
#> # A tibble: 6 × 2
#>   Gene    ScaledLog2FC
#>   <chr>          <dbl>
#> 1 POLR2L         -2.23
#> 2 POLR3H         -2.15
#> 3 GPN3           -2.11
#> 4 ISG20L2        -1.94
#> 5 RRM1           -1.93
#> 6 MRPL53         -1.91

Positive-selection screens

In a drug-resistance or positive-selection screen the interesting genes are enriched: their knockout makes the cells survive. Every hit-finding function takes direction = "Up":

find_gene_zscore_hit(statistics, direction = "Up")
find_camera_hit(object, design, contrast, direction = "Up")

The reference genes are not useful there (they describe fitness, not resistance); use the default reference of find_gene_zscore_hit() or control genes known to have no effect on the selection.

Summary

Step CRISPR-specific advice Functions
Create the object describe time points with a sample_table create_screenr_object()
sgRNAs per gene lower number_barcode / min_barcodes for 3-6 sgRNAs per gene barcodes_per_gene()
Quality control check the separation of essential and non-essential genes compute_screen_quality(), plot_reference_separation()
Copy-number bias correct with CRISPRcleanR on the complete library correct_crispr_bias()
Hits use the non-essential genes as reference when available, otherwise the empirical null find_gene_zscore_hit(control_genes = ), find_gene_zscore_hit(reference = "empirical"), plot_empirical_null(), find_camera_hit(), find_roast_hit(), summarise_hits()
Compare screens scale to the reference genes scale_by_reference()
Positive selection look for enriched genes direction = "Up"

Literature

  • Hart T, Tong AHY, Chan K et al. (2017). Evaluation and design of genome-wide CRISPR/SpCas9 knockout screens. G3 7:2719-2727.
  • Hart T, Brown KR, Sircoulomb F, Rottapel R, Moffat J (2014). Measuring error rates in genomic perturbation screens: gold standards for human functional genomics. Mol Syst Biol 10:733.
  • Iorio F, Behan FM, Goncalves E et al. (2018). Unsupervised correction of gene-independent cell responses to CRISPR-Cas9 targeting. BMC Genomics 19:604.
